children.text: This article delves into the positive impacts of recycling and demolition of construction materials on both the environment and the economy. children.text: Summary: This article presents a case study on the ecological benefits of selective demolition in construction waste management. By examining real-world projects and data, we assess the positive impact of selective demolition on waste reduction, recovery of reusable materials, and conservation of natural resources. Furthermore, we discuss best practices and provide recommendations for promoting selective demolition in the construction industry, emphasizing its long-term ecological and economic advantages. Through this analysis, we aim to encourage the adoption of sustainable practices and innovative solutions for effective waste management in construction projects.

children.text: The circular economy is a transformative approach to sustainable development, moving away from the traditional 'take-make-dispose' model towards a system that is restorative and regenerative. This article explores the core principles of the circular economy—designing out waste, keeping materials in use, and regenerating natural systems. It highlights the significant environmental, economic, and social benefits, along with real-world applications in industries such as automotive, fashion, and electronics. The Netherlands serves as a leading example, demonstrating successful national initiatives. Despite challenges, the circular economy offers a promising path to sustainability, requiring collective effort from governments, businesses, and consumers.

title.en: The Circular Economy: A Pathway to Sustainable Development

children.text: The building sector is a major contributor to global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the sector accounted for roughly 39% of global CO2 emissions related to energy in 2020. These emissions are split into two main categories:
Operational Emissions
: About 28% of emissions come from the operation of buildings, including heating, cooling, lighting, and more.
Embodied Emissions
: Around 11% are linked to the production of construction materials and the actual building process.

title.en: The Urgency of Building Low-Carbon Buildings

children.text: This article highlights the ecological and economic benefits of selective demolition in construction waste management. By carefully dismantling structures to recover reusable materials, selective demolition reduces waste, conserves resources, and lowers the carbon footprint of projects. Economically, it saves on disposal costs, generates revenue from salvaged materials, and creates job opportunities. Case studies from cities like Portland and Copenhagen showcase the success of these practices. The article emphasizes the need for policy support, education, and technological investment to promote selective demolition, driving sustainability in the construction industry.

title.en: The Ecological and Economic Advantages of Selective Demolition in Construction Waste Management

Recycled asphalt, or reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP), is made by blending
materials from old pavements with new binders and aggregates. This eco-friendly
solution reduces the need for virgin resources, cutting costs and minimizing
environmental impact. It offers durable, high-performance roads with lower
maintenance requirements. Recycling can be done on-site or at specialized
plants, depending on project needs. However, strict quality control and material
testing are essential to ensure the final product meets safety and durability
standards.
